The difficulty is economic: the option to default makes the borrower&apos;s problem non-concave, and long maturities make the bond price a fixed point that feeds policy errors back into prices. We compare extreme-value taste shocks on a discrete menu with interpolated continuous-choice optimization in the Chatterjee and Eyigungor (2012) one-asset model and the Bianchi, Hatchondo and Martinez (2018) reserves model, both validated against the published replication outputs. First, smoothing the choice rule distorts primarily portfolio composition rather than leverage: reserves vary sharply with the taste-shock scale while mean debt barely moves—an error a one-asset model cannot exhibit. Second, convergence and accuracy are distinct. Borrower Euler residuals, lender pricing residuals, and a global menu-deviation audit reveal converged solutions that violate the model’s optimality conditions, a non-converged terminal iterate that matches converged candidates on the scored conditions, and matched moments—the literature’s usual check—that mask an order of magnitude in first-order accuracy. Third, taste shocks solve the portfolio model roughly three to four times faster than the continuous-choice reference at a small welfare cost, and a single post-solve re-optimization of the actions, repriced and re-evaluated, eliminates the measured welfare gap with the reference. An exact factorization of the pricing recursion contributes to the implementation’s speed.</jats:p>\",…

id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16021v1
published: 2025-04-22T16:35:39Z
summary: Flow theory describes an optimal cognitive state where individuals experience deep focus and intrinsic motivation when a task's difficulty aligns with their skill level. In AI-augmented reasoning, interventions that disrupt the state of cognitive flow can hinder rather than enhance decision-making. This paper proposes a context-aware cognitive augmentation framework that adapts interventions based on three key contextual factors: type, timing, and scale. By leveraging multimodal behavioral cues (e.g., gaze behavior, typing hesitation, interaction speed), AI can dynamically adjust cognitive support to maintain or restore flow. We introduce the concept of cognitive flow, an extension of flow theory in AI-augmented reasoning, where interventions are personalized, adaptive, and minimally intrusive. By shifting from static interventions to context-aware augmentation, our approach ensures that AI systems support deep engagement in complex decision-making and reasoning without disrupting cognitive immersion.
